title: pranayama sequences
hook: in an Upanishad the body's powers argue over who holds it up, until the breath gets up to leave
carry: like bees with the king bee

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita ended on one word, kva, where, and the lineage track closed: karma, bhakti, jnana. Today, a new stretch: practices, deeper.

The powers of the body are having an argument. Speech says it holds the body up. The eye says no, it does. The ear, the mind, the elements themselves all make the same boast. It's a scene from the Prashna Upanishad, told by a teacher named Pippalada to a student who asked which powers keep a living being going. In the middle of the shouting, one power gives a single warning and stops arguing. The breath. Prana. Nobody believes it, so it simply gets up, as if to leave.
screen: `THE BODY'S POWERS ARGUE.` → `EACH ONE BOASTS.` → `THE BREATH GETS UP TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's what happens next, in paraphrase. Prana, the chief power, has warned them: don't be fooled, I'm the one holding this body together. They don't believe it, so prana rises to go. As it rises, every other power is pulled up with it, helpless to stay. When it settles back down, they all settle, like bees that rise when the king bee rises and settle when it settles. The argument is over. Speech, mind, eye and ear turn to prana and praise it. That story sits under this whole week. Pranayama is the name for practices that work with prana by way of the breath. If everything else rises and settles with the breath, then working with the breath works with the rest too: the restless mind, the racing heart, the scattered attention. These days take the practices as sequences, one step after another in an order, gentle ones before stronger ones. Two warnings belong right at the start. Breath practice is done gently: nothing forced, nothing held until it hurts. If there's dizziness or strain, stop and breathe normally. And anyone with a heart or lung condition, or who is pregnant, talks to a doctor before trying the stronger practices. Today there's nothing strong at all. Just the king bee, rising and settling, and everything else going with it.
screen: `PRANA RISES; EVERYTHING RISES.` · `LIKE BEES WITH THE KING BEE.` · `PRANAYAMA: WORKING WITH PRANA.` · `A SEQUENCE: ONE STEP AFTER ANOTHER.` · then, large: `GENTLY. NOTHING FORCED.`

segments.voice: Sit with the spine easy and watch the breath rise and settle without changing it, noticing what goes with it: the belly, the ribs, the shoulders, even the thoughts. After a while, let the out-breath become just a little slower than before, still easy. If anything strains, let it go back to normal.
Pranayama sequences: breath practices set in an order, working with prana, the power the others rise and settle with.
Your line: like bees with the king bee. In the story, when the breath settles, everything settles with it. Day one thousand five.

howItsDone: Pranayama is traditionally learned from a teacher; in many lineages a session begins sitting upright after some posture work, starting with gentle breath awareness and slow exhalation before any breath retention, and stopping at any dizziness or strain.

chat.says: Why start a breathing practice with a story about body parts arguing?
options: It shows prana as the power the others rise and settle with, so breath reaches the rest.
It shows speech is the strongest power, so chanting matters most of all.
It shows the body's powers never agree, so practice has to force them.
chat.meaning: In the Prashna Upanishad, when prana rises every power rises with it. So working with the breath works with mind and heart too.
